utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Krajisnik, we received a small bundle again this morning that has been given to the parties. I see that there are quite some -- quite some newspaper articles in it. There are a few documents in it as well, but before I perhaps ask you a question about it, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I see that there's one -- there seems to be a decision of the 28th of December, 1991, appointing certain people on a staff. Could you please tell us what that approximately is about. It's got to do something with Omarska, it comes from the opstina of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's a document that is perhaps useful; namely that Omarska was first a collection centre for refugees from Croatia in 1991. That is when it was established. So I wanted to submit it as a useful document. It was the local commune that established Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then there is another document from August, 1992, from Prijedor and signed by Simo Drljaca. Could you tell us what that document is approximately about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, he describes Omarska and Keraterm as prisons and Trnopolje as a collection centre. So I just wanted to indicate what kind of information we were receiving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you did receive these documents at that time, is that -- perhaps we'll put them on the ELMO for a second. Just the numbers --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't get it at the time. I just found them, Your Honour. At that time, I heard somebody providing information about Trnopolje, so I just wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but of course the relevance would be that that's information that reached you at the time. Yes. Let's first look at this. Could I invite -- I know that it's not the preferred way to do it, but could I invite the first five lines to be slowly read by you, Mr. Krajisnik, and then we'll hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Assembly Prijedor, Executive Council of the local commune of Omarska, Omarska, 28 December, 1991. "Decision. "At a meeting of the Executive Council, a decision was reached on the establishment of a staff for taking in refugees named Omarska in cooperation with the Executive Councils of the local communities of Omarska, Maricka, Gradina, Lamovita, Donji Petrov Gaj and Gornji Petrov Gaj and in cooperation with the regional staff of Banja Luka." Should I read on? "A commander was elected --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that it's all names and -- yes. Mr. Krajisnik, this says something that happened -- well, refugees in Omarska, but when we're talking about Omarska camp, that's not the same as just Omarska, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. No. I meant that already then there was some kind of facility that was established for refugees, and later on it was turned into a camp. That is what I concluded, and I thought you'd find it useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What makes you believe that this is not Omarska village and it is -- because there is no reference whatsoever to what later became known as Omarska camp, which is at quite a distance from the village, very much remote.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. This is the Executive Council of Omarska, that is to say the entire settlement of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but again who tells us that this -- that what has been set up here was located at this -- at this facility which is at quite a distance from the village, and which is -- which was, from what I understand, was just functioning as a -- as an economic facility, a mine, an ore mine. Who tells us that this was the same? What it says, that it is in Omarska, but it doesn't say anything about whether it's in the ore mine, which is at - well, what is it? - two kilometres? Totally remote from the village of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I brought the document, and I provided an interpretation that I cannot stand by. You will decide whether it's relevant or not. I just wanted to be of assistance, that's all. I first saw it here when I read the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the second document. This -- this would need a number. I don't know whether the parties want to adopt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm happy to invite the registrar through Your Honour to give it a D number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar, that would be D --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 251, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 251. Now, the next document, Mr. Krajisnik, you say in this -- in this document signed by Mr. Drljaca he makes a distinction between -- and that's in August, 1992 -- he makes a distinction between -- between the reception centre at Trnopolje, whereas Omarska and Keraterm are called prisons. Of course, I -- I take it at this moment you can read it; you provided the document. And you said, "I gave it to you to tell you what kind of information," and -- let me see your words literally. I have to find it, please wait a second. You said, "So I just wanted to indicate what kind of information we were receiving," and then you said you didn't receive this at this moment. What it says, therefore, is that although Trnopolje is, as you said - and let's just assume that that's what the translation would bring us - was called a reception centre, at the same time Omarska and Keraterm, as you said, were called prisons. So is -- do you say, "That's the information we got," Trnopolje being reception centre and the others to be called prisons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know when it was that I first heard of Trnopolje, but whenever I received information, a distinction was always made between Omarska and Trnopolje. Trnopolje was called a reception centre. That's what I wanted to say, that there is a document, but then there are other documents referring to it the same way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Omarska you received always information that it was called a prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, I mean -- well, you will see this other document here. When journalists visited, Keraterm, Omarska and Manjaca were prisons and Trnopolje was a reception centre. I mean, that's how they reported. So that was the information I was receiving at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say at the time Manjaca, Keraterm and Omarska, you were aware that these were named prisons, whereas Trnopolje was named a reception centre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I knew it. I received information when this was revealed, when journalists toured this, when this commission provided a report, when they made a distinction among the three. That's when I received information that there was a reception centre and that there are prisons in Prijedor. Later on -- well, really, I can give you several documents stating that Trnopolje was a reception centre. I cannot claim that. I just read it here, and I heard about it from people who were saying that it was an open centre. What I wanted to say was that I wanted you to know what kind of impression you got when you would receive information. I was not there. I don't know what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's -- Mr. Josse, you offer for this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This document, I noticed, Your Honour, has a Tribunal number on it, and I've just checked and that number refers, unsurprisingly, to the very case that has the subname Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje camps. So it's almost certainly been translated, in other words. But again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we then invite to see whether ... Then we have some newspaper articles. I leave it to the parties to see if there is any use, because there seem to be some contemporaneous and there seem to be some publications later. I see one is October, 1995. So what that would have meant is not entirely clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's got the same number, I noticed, Your Honour; IT-98-30 on the top of it. Both of them have, so the material could have been disclosed somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't see these numbers at this moment, but that's not a major problem. And then we also have at least one publication which seems to be Kozarski Vjesnik, dated --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 14th of August. That's it. And it refers to seven days before that, to the visit paid by the journalists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see -- I see, as a matter of fact, but perhaps I'm wrong, I also see the 21st of August mentioned as a date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There is another one dated the 21st of August. That has to do with Mr. Kouchner, who visited these prisons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave that to the parties whether or not to enter -- to see --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could the document that's dated 9th of August, 1992, be assigned a number? We've spent a little bit of time on it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D252, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, and let's try to find out whether there's a translation already in existence. Mr. Tieger, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Before we conclude the questions that we were engaged in yesterday concerning camps and exchanges and so on, I wanted to ask you one quick question about your testimony on the 25th of May when you stated that for personal reasons you were not present in Pale on August 23rd and for several days before and after that. In fact, Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like you to take a look at the next document, which will need a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We find it at tab -- it's still to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And, Your Honour, I'm referring to May 25th, at page 24789.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give one or two words very specific from those lines, because I've got no --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "And several days before and after ..." I'm sorry, I didn't hear the number it was provided.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P 1249, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, P 1249 is an article from Javnost dated 29 August, 1992, it's page 3, and if you will look at the article in the upper right-hand portion of the page headed "Momcilo Krajisnik congratulated SRNA on their Jubilee." The title of the article is "Battle for the Truth." And it indicates that: "On Saturday, 22 August, president of the Assembly of Republika Srpska Momcilo Krajisnik received in Pale the deputy editor-in-chief of the Serbian news agency SRNA Dragan Gardovic. On that occasion he congratulated the SRNA staff on the broadcast of their 5.000th news item." It would appear therefore, Mr. Krajisnik, that in fact you were present in Pale at least on August 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't there on the 22nd of August for sure, because then I took my wife to the Military Medical Academy in Belgrade. I have no idea how come this appeared on the 22nd when she died early on the morning of the 23rd. I was in Belgrade. I have no idea where this comes from. If you want, I can give you proof and documentation stating when I was in Belgrade. I know for sure that I was not there. I don't know how come it says the 22nd here. Maybe they got their dates confused. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I indicated that we were going to continue focusing on the area --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it necessary for me to bring documentation to you as to when I was in Belgrade and everything, when she died, all of that? If you have your suspicions regarding this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I stop Mr. Krajisnik. I, frankly, was very tempted in effect on his behalf to ask my learned friend the same question. I don't expect an answer now, but perhaps we could have one after the break, because clearly if it is in dispute, then it's something Mr. Krajisnik will need to attend to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Your Honour, I am not going to respond to questions from Mr. Krajisnik. I appreciate Mr. Josse's intervention. And secondly, the information before the Court is apparent, and if the Defence is inclined to produce additional documentation, obviously it's welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would submit that's remarkably unhelpful, with respect, and the Prosecution need to pin their colours to the mast on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider whether it will give guidance to the parties in respect of a matter which, although now -- although not without importance might not be of such importance that what certainly will be a rather painful exercise would be needed to correct this. We'll consider the matter, and please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, as I indicated, we're returning to the issue we were discussing yesterday. As I recall, towards the end of the session you had been presented with and looked at the commission report regarding Omarska, Keraterm, Trnopolje camps in Sanski Most and other places in Western Bosnia, and we addressed that report to some extent at the end. Now, you also indicated that there were two additional reports that reflected the strict and resolute action by the Presidency in response to the outcry by the international community and the disclosure that -- worldwide, of the existence of Bosnian Serb camps in which Muslims and Croats were held. The next document I'd like you to look at, then, is an additional document. It's a report in August of 1992 to which you've earlier referred, report by Slobodan Avlijas. That would need to be distributed, Your Honour, and it is P583, tab 92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While it is distributed: Mr. Krajisnik, do you know Javnost, whether it was a daily newspaper or a weekly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a weekly, yes, a weekly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar, this needs a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour; P583, tab 92.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Krajisnik, this document to the government of the Serb republic by the Republika Srpska Ministry of Justice for Mr. Avlijas and Mr. Saric, that was one of the three documents, the three reports concerning camps to which you've been referring during the course of your testimony about the camps and the action taken by the Presidency in response; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report issued by a government commission. They are from the Ministry of Justice, and they were directly tasked by the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And to my knowledge, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the question was whether this is one of the documents you referred to, not to disquiet the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what we saw yesterday was the commission investigation into camps in Western Bosnia in August, and this is the investigation by the authorities into camps in Eastern Bosnia, I take it, in August. I know there is a subsequent report in late October, but this would be the Eastern Bosnia version of the effort made in the wake of the disclosures in early August; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. This is a report from Herzegovina. That's the southern part, Herzegovina. Bileca, that's Eastern Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So Posusje camp, for example, in Vlasenica would not have been included in the efforts made by the Bosnian Serb authorities in August to find out what was happening in camps run by the Bosnian Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a commission for Eastern Herzegovina. Whether it was also, therefore, Birac and Eastern Bosnia, I don't know, but probably, yes. However, it says here that it's for Herzegovina. I read this report when I arrived here, so I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. And like the report concerning Manjaca, Omarska, Keraterm, et cetera, this report, according to you, is a reflection of the determination by the Bosnian Serb authorities to find out what was happening in camps and who was responsible. So what was happening, whether misconduct had occurred, how prisoners had been treated and who was responsible and accountable if wrongful detentions and abuse had occurred; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was the decisive standpoint of the Presidency where I was present, and an order was issued to the government to complete this, and a commission was established to tour the terrain. So I can only assume, but I presume yes. When I was present at the Presidency, there was a decisive standpoint that this should be investigated, and an order was given to the government to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And after taking this decisive standpoint, Mr. Krajisnik, what did the Presidency or other authorities in Bosnian -- in Republika Srpska do when they got this report about camps, this one-page, one-paragraph report that said essentially, Here there's no camp; here there are two camps; here there are no prisoners now. There were no prisoners in the barracks, it says, in Bileca since all the prisoners had been exchanged in the all-for-all principle the day before. Where in this - and you can read it very quickly - where in this report is there any indication of an interest in determining what happened to the people who were there, why they were, and who was responsible?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you that I did not receive this report. I read it here, just as you did. I can tell you what action was taken. You will recall that the government had a closed session about all these reports, and after that the remaining prisons were disbanded. I know that. Mr. Karadzic issued an order disbanding them, and this was sometime in August. You have it there, the 46th government session in Banja Luka, where all these reports were discussed. This report was discussed by the cabinet. It wasn't disseminated. It was received on the 22nd of August, I see. After that, the prisons were disbanded. The cabinet had a discussion, and then the president of the republic disbanded the prisons. I don't know whether he -- all of them were abolished, but he released a large number of people and so on. You can find all this in the Presidency minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll be looking at the Presidency minutes, Mr. Krajisnik. All right. But my question was, what steps, if any, are you aware of that were taken to find out why the prisoners were there, what happened to them while they were there, and who was responsible, and I take it you can't tell me about any.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you now what I read here. Then the government formed commissions to make a tour --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me make it clear: I want to know what steps you were aware of at the time that were being taken to address that issue first.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that the government was tasked with carrying out this task, and the order was that the truth should be established.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And do you know of any steps other than the three reports you've told us about, because I'm about to turn to the third report.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe I knew something at the time, but that was unofficial. Officially, I knew nothing. Officially, it was all at cabinet level, and the government worked on this persistently. I know that the president of the government, the ministers and the others, kept insisting on it. And how the commission did its job, well, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, you said, "[In English] Officially, I knew nothing."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is the following: Do you mean by this that you had unofficial knowledge or informed in an unofficial way? Does it also mean that you had a certain number of information -- you had some information but that that information had not arrived to you by official means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an official document. I did not receive such a document for my information. I don't exclude the possibility that while the government was working on this someone said something about it, but I don't remember having received any such information while the commission was at work. Had I received it, it would have been at the Assembly or somewhere. That's my answer. If I had received this and discussed it, but I didn't, not until it was all over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, if you had received those documents, for instance, would you have been happy with them? Would you have examined them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wouldn't have been. I would have asked for a debate to see what could be done, and if there was anything negative, I would have demanded that those who were responsible should take steps. But I was not able to punish anyone or take any steps. I could only demand that the government do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but my question was not exactly that. If we take this report, I would call it very succinct, it's a very short report. It's not an investigation report, per se. The Prosecutor asked you a question regarding this. There's no real investigation on what happened, there's no real hearing as to see who was responsible for anything, there was no real work done by investigators who then at the end of that particular phase created or drafted a report. And I haven't finished. I'm terribly sorry for interrupting you, Mr. Krajisnik, but my question is the following: If you had had such a succinct report, what would have been your reaction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As someone who is close to those who are responsible, I could only influence them or suggest that this should be fuller, but I could not ask for a report on my own. The Presidency could do that. I could speak out within the Presidency, and that was the end of all my activity. I couldn't punish. I couldn't not trust the government if the government issued a conclusion. I could say, Wait a minute, is this correct? if there were any indications elsewhere that this was not the case, but there was nothing I could do. Had I had any indications, had I heard, well, it's not 25, it's 150, then I could say something, but without such indications I could only believe them as someone who participated in a meeting where this was discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you said if not all, then at least almost all prisons were disbanded. Were you informed about that? Did you know that they were disbanded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, Mr. Karadzic took some measures. I know he released 5.000 prisoners. That's why I think all prisons were disbanded, but I cannot recall now what prisons and whether it was really all of them. I may have spoken too decidedly when I said all. If the Muslims did not want to carry out an exchange, our people were left in Muslim prisons, and I know that some measures were taken. Karadzic released these people one-sidedly because he was under pressure, while the other side did not want to carry out an exchange and Serbs remained in Muslim prisons. That's why I know about this, and you'll probably find this somewhere. If I had the minutes here, I would find it. It was a unilateral decision taken by Mr. Karadzic. I know he released about 5.000 people. I think it was from Trnopolje, but I'm not sure. I don't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's one facility you're talking about. You said that after that, the prisons were disbanded. We know that there were far more. At least, that's what the evidence suggests. I mean, if -- I asked you whether you knew that the prisons were disbanded, and you then said perhaps not all of them. Now you're talking about the release of 5.000 people from Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my information when Mr. Karadzic unilaterally disbanded prisons - I don't know which - and released the Muslims, I know there were complaints by Serbs. That's how I know about all this, because the Muslims had not released the Serbs, and now we could not ask for an exchange and get our Serbs back. But I don't know now off the top of my head, but I could find in the documents which prisons were disbanded and which were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm interested in what you knew at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew that he released a certain number of people, 5.000. I may have exaggerated this, but I know that there were complaints about this decision of his and that we could not carry out exchanges of prisoners and that deputies were complaining about that. I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you share that criticism? Whether you expressed it or not is a different matter, but did you share that criticism?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I listened to all the information from all three sides, and I was sorry that Serbs had remained in Muslim prisons because we had agreed that an all-for-all exchange should be carried out. Of course I was concerned about the Serbs. I would have preferred there to have been an exchange rather than a unilateral release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you to some extent shared that criticism. You think that an exchange should have taken place rather than a release. I mean, you're -- you say whether you agree or did not agree with those who criticised Mr. Karadzic for what he did, or to some extent -- do I have to understand that to some extent that you shared the criticism but perhaps not in full or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I supported Mr. Karadzic. I knew why he had done this, but I regretted that an exchange had not been carried out and that the Serbs remained in prison. I knew that he had been under pressure and that he had to release those people. Others didn't know that, and so they criticised him for not carrying out an exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Pressure by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Sommaruga, various foreigners, and then he said, "All right, I'll release them all, and I think that the Muslims will do the same unilaterally on the other side," but the Muslims didn't. It was the representatives of the international community who continued exerting pressure to have the Muslims released after all those visits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there no criticism that Mr. Karadzic released people that belonged in a prison, that should be prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why would Mr. Karadzic release those who were rightfully in a prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He released many people who should have remained in prison. He released them all. He said, "All right. We will release them all because we want an all-for-all exchange, and I hope that now the Muslims will release our prisoners." I know that's how it happened. He didn't release only those who shouldn't have been in prison. I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there was an awareness at that time that there were also people in prison who should not have been there. You said he released both the ones who should have been in prison and the others. So there was awareness of people being in prison who should not have been there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. You asked whether he had released those who should have been released and who shouldn't have been released. I said he released them all because he wanted an all-for-all exchange. He released them all. I don't know who these people were. And then the Muslims were to have done the same, but they didn't. The international community said that they would, but they didn't. There should have been an all-for-all exchange, and that would have been the end of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your answer was he didn't release only those who shouldn't have been in prison. That seems to be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was responding to your question, Your Honour, whether he had released those who should have remained in prison and shouldn't have remained. I said he let them all out. I didn't know whether they should or shouldn't have been in prison. He released everyone, hoping there would be an all-for-all exchange. I don't know whether there were people in there who shouldn't have been in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You didn't know whether -- yes. Okay. Thank you for those answers. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, please turn to tab 312. That's P583, tab 100. This is a report on the situation in prisons and collection camps from the RS Ministry of Justice dated 22 October, 1992. Mr. Krajisnik, is this the other, that is the third, commission report to which you've been referring during the course of your testimony regarding this issue?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what number it is, but I have seen it here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you don't know what number it is? Does that mean -- are you aware of any other reports, other than the three we've looked at, that were responses to what you called the decisive steps of the Presidency after the international outcry about camps?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the way you put the question is completely wrong. I don't know why you're putting words into my mouth. I said I saw this report when I arrived here. I don't know whether it's the second or the third report. I don't know. We saw three reports here which you presented yesterday and today. Now there is a third one here. I don't know whether there are any other reports. If you show me any other reports, I will be able to tell you whether I saw them or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's a very long way of answering my question, Mr. Krajisnik. I asked you whether you were aware of any additional reports. The answer was no; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seem to have been -- there seem to have been --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not what you asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik. There seems to have been to some extent a mistranslation when the number was mentioned. Well, mistranslation, perhaps not a translation that made the words of Mr. Krajisnik fully understandable, which is that he doesn't know whether it was the second or the third. The first question, however, was a very simple question, Mr. Krajisnik, that has been put to you before: That this is one of the reports that you referred to earlier. If you would have said yes, because then whether it was the second or the third might have been important, might not have been important. Is this one of the reports you referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not the question. The question was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... was the first question, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The problem, with respect, was Mr. Tieger asked two questions at the same time, and that is where the difficulty arose. He first asked about the number, and then he asked about whether there were subsequent reports. There's actually a question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll re-read it so that I ... Yes. I do agree with you that the question was a mixed one --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which is whether it was the third report --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was the first question. When he started to make that an issue, I simply asked, Are you aware of any other reports?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. By the way, it's -- I wouldn't call it a comedy of errors, but of course then Mr. Krajisnik, when he said, "I don't know what number it is," he didn't say, "But it is the report I referred to." He didn't say that but "I have seen it here," which is of course not the same as I referred to, whether it was the second or third. Let's proceed and let's not spend any more time on misunderstandings. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's try that again, Mr. Krajisnik. This report at tab 12 -- 312, which is P583, tab 100, was this one of the reports that was a response to what you called the decisive steps taken by the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, I saw this report for the first time here. I can assume that, yes, that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other steps to determine what was happening in camps, how people, Muslims and Croats, had been placed there and why, whether abuse had occurred, and who was responsible other than the three reports we've looked at today and yesterday? That is, the report by Beara and Skondric in August of 1992 -- and others, in August of 1992 regarding Omarska, Keraterm, Krings, et cetera, the report by Avlijas we looked at a few moments ago, and this report by Avlijas on October 22nd, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive these reports at the time. That's the first correction I want to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the question is relative simple, that is, whether you are aware of any other than the three reports mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there were some military reports presented at some meeting, if I attended, perhaps I heard about it, but then measures were taken immediately. I know that. I was never at a meeting where measures were not taken. I think there was this one report from the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say there may have been more reports among the military --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I mean honestly I don't know whether the interpreter is interpreting this properly. I am speaking so clearly. Perhaps there was some report from the military. Perhaps. If I was present, then I heard it and measures were certainly taken. I always keep getting the wrong reaction as if I were saying something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I do not see a major difference with how I summarised it, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see the difference. There's always a tendentious difference and a tendentious question. I give clear answers to clear questions, and tendentious questions upset me. Today the Prosecutor keeps putting words into my mouth, and he says things that are wrong. A public that is being upset or was upset or whatever. To clear questions I will give clear answers, yes, no, I did not know. Please do not put words into my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is that right, Mr. Krajisnik, you're disputing that the international community was - what are your words? - upset by the disclosures concerning Omarska, Keraterm, and so on? Was I wrong in suggesting in any way that that was the case?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wrong. And I told you very nicely that there were complaints, that the delegation went there, that journalists went there, that there was writing about it, and that there were contacts all the time, and objections, objections, and that people from the government kept denying that, saying that that was not correct. That is the truth. That's what I said. It's not being upset, it's simply complaints. And being upset is quite different from objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, please turn to tab 306 -- oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, at the time was it possible to think that the president of the National Assembly, in other words yourself, could you have taken an initiative? For instance, could you have designated members of the parliament deputies to make an investigation regarding something that you could call rumours, troublesome rumours or rumours that were unsettling, that those rumours, for instance whether they were rumours that came from the international community or whether you heard rumours internally, for instance, could you have done something? Thank you. Yes, please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Presidency of the Assembly and the Assembly had commissions, and within their own province of work they could investigate certain matters, and they did indeed investigate a particular matter. As for this particular matter, they could not because this was under the jurisdiction of the government. It would have to interfere with the powers of the government. It was for the government to investigate this, to submit a report to the Assembly; we were supposed to discuss that. That is the proper channel. It would be that we were interfering in the province of work of someone who was in charge of that. We sent a commission to investigate the rumours that had to do with Mr. Simic and Mr. Bijelic. We indeed did that because that was within our jurisdiction. We were not supposed to check out prisons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not like to start a debate on constitutional law here, but tell us, please, can the Assembly not also control, in a way, the actions of the government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but really, that would have been very unusual. If there is a government commission -- if you were to send an Assembly commission consisting of MPs to control the work of the government, that kind of thing never happened. They could only check on the work of the government within the Assembly, but they could not go after the government. I don't know whether that exists somewhere else, but it never existed in our area. You have to believe someone. If you don't believe anyone, that will lead you nowhere. It's only if I followed every single person around, seeing that they were doing. That's impossible. Then I would also have to check on this Assembly commission, and so on and so forth, and that is quite impossible. That has nothing to do with the Assembly. It has to do with the government, so that's what the government did. Perhaps all of this is wrong, but this is what the Prime Minister received. The Prime Minister could not have received any other kind of information, only this. And those people from the commission could only receive what they got from the ground, what they were told there. That's how UN commissions work too. They come, they interview people, they see what the situation is. Very often they make mistakes too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, please turn to tab 306.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It will need a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1250, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, P1250 reflects a meeting at Manjaca on 20 August, 1992, concerning the views on the treatment and processing of the persons who participated in armed rebellion. Participants are Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, the camp commander; Major Stupar, the coordinator of the 1st Krajina security organ; Vaso Skondric, and we've seen before as a participant in one of the investigative visions; and Radomir Radinkovic. As you can see on the first page, Mr. Krajisnik, Major Stupar made introductory remarks about the views of the Presidency of Republika Srpska, and he said: "List of 92 persons for whom there is no evidence that they carried out - participated in combat activities and who have serious health problems and attract the attention of journalists and the representatives of humanitarian organisations because of their physical appearance." And then the task is to consider their status for these reasons. And we see a list of such people attached. And just going through it quickly, we see Mr. Alibegovic, who had a stroke, Mr. Pobric who had one hand, Mr. Salihovic who had active pulmonary tuberculosis, Mr. Mehmet Sistek who had diabetes and could not stand up - that's on page 5 of the English. Page 6, Mr. Fazlic who had an operation of the large intestine and no control over bowel movement. Mr. Dedic, kidney disease, and so on and so on and so on. Before I go -- Mr. Krajisnik, when did the Presidency convey to Major Stupar the views of that body concerning the treatment and processing of prisoners for whom there is no evidence that they carried out or were involved in combat activities and whose medical condition and health problems were attracting the attention of journalists and representatives of humanitarian organisations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. That can be seen in the records. But I know that part of these activities aimed at releasing the elderly were based on Mr. Karadzic's order, as far as I can remember. But you can see in the records whether there is such a discussion. Probably after the return of Mr. Ostojic and this commission. They probably established that independently from the commission, and they proposed that. If it was in the Presidency, then it's there. If not, then he did it at his own initiative, and he had the right to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, there are -- the list, the P1250, also indicates persons who were known not to have had any alleged involvement at all in what is called here armed rebellion but who -- whose medical conditions apparently weren't attracting the attention of journalists and representatives of humanitarian organisations, and we see that at page 15 of the English and page 15 of the B/C/S. It's one of the tasks following Major Stupar's contact with the Presidency concerning their views, and that is to review the list of 400 persons for whom there is no evidence that they committed the crime of armed rebellion in cooperation with civilian authorities, hand-over at reception camps, or other type of accommodations -- accommodation. That was another step that, following contact with the Presidency, that the officials at Manjaca were engaged in or considering on 20 August, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably if it's contained in the records of the Presidency, then yes, but I don't know. I mean, this way -- well, I find this to be normal, this order that those for whom there is no evidence should be released. Many people get detained, and they think that they have evidence for that, and then they start collecting evidence, and then ultimately they get released. And some people get released even when there is evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, here it's not a case of thinking there's evidence. Here it says there's no evidence. So it's apparent, is it not, that at least these 400, if not others, were among those people who were rounded up as indicated, for example, in Mr. Stanisic's 17 July, 1992, report to the Presidency -- or to the president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Many people get detained in even more serious prisons, and it is only then that evidence is compiled and then it is presented at trials. If there is no evidence, then they are released. I'm just saying this by way of a comment. Of course, if there is no evidence, they should be released.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we look at the list of people falling into that overlap category, that is people against whom there is no evidence and whose medical conditions are so severe that they are attracting the negative attention of the international community, we can see the dates of their -- at the beginning of their detention, such as 29 May, 1992, and 31 --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Is that at the beginning of the text? Could you please just tell me where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's the list that appears immediately after the comments by -- concerning the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. These tasks, assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So just leafing through quickly, we see Nermin Pobric captured on 29 May, 1992; Mehmed Sistek 27 May, 1992, that's page 4; Mr. Salihovic 29 May, 1992, on page 5; Mr. Draganovic 31 May, 1992, also on page 5; Mr. Vuckic, on page 6, 27 May, 1992; Mr. Dervisevic 29 May, 1992, and so on. So those were persons against whom there was no evidence and whose medical condition was so severe as to attract or be capable of attracting the attention of journalists and representatives who had been in prisons and detention facilities for months and were still being considered for release because of the attention they were attracting or potential attention they might attract by the international community; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what's written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you mention one of the Presidency sessions. Could we turn next to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. -- Mr. Krajisnik, part of your answer was that it was -- that you considered it to be normal that if there was no evidence that you would release the people and you would not know right from the beginning. If I look at this document, it says that the 92 people who are apparently visibly ill or in bad condition, and where there is no evidence, they should be released, but other, the other 400 - that's at page 15 - to review the list of 400 persons for whom there's no evidence that they committed the crime of armed rebellion in cooperation with civilian authorities, hand-over at reception camps or other types of accommodations. Why were they not immediately released if there was no evidence? Why were only those who were visibly ill immediately released? As for the others without any evidence, they should be handed over to collection centres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to be released from prison here and to be accommodated. I don't know about this. But for all of those for whom there was no evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you permitted yourself to say this was quite normal, so you commented on this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I'm now asking you, since you -- since you gave this comment, whether this comment is -- where it says that it's quite normal, I'm asking you not about the 92 that were immediately released but whether you consider it then normal for the 400 people who were not immediately released and who were sent to reception centres rather than to have the same opportunity to leave the prison immediately. It says that there was no evidence. Do you find that normal as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was normal for them to be set free if they had not been set free. It is only normal. If there is no evidence, they should be set free. They should be released. And had I been the one to be asked, I would have released all the rest too. And I can explain why I would have done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. We're more interested whether you have an explanation why it was not done to the 400.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. No. I do not have an explanation, but it's only normal that they should be released. Because there is no evidence, then they should be released. Why would they be in prison? Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Allow only those who could be identified by journalists as being unfit to be there for release, and the others, although there was no evidence, were not released. And would you agree with me that that is what is described in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what is written in the document, but I don't know. I did not know of this document, but there were views that all should be released, not only these but the others too. That's what I'm trying to say. Mr. President, can I just say something, why I would have released the others for whom there was evidence? May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. As a matter of fact, unless Mr. Josse wants to put that question to you at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The very last question Your Honour asked, could I ask Your Honour to ask it again? It doesn't read easily in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I briefly described who were released, who were not released, and then I asked Mr. Krajisnik whether -- and would you agree with me that that is described in this document? So whether we have the same understanding of what this document says. That was my question. And then Mr. Krajisnik said, "That is was -- that is what was written in the documents, but," and then he said he didn't know the document and that there were other views. But I was just trying to establish whether we have a similar understanding as to what this document says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Mr. President, I beg your pardon. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I gave an answer to an issue that was raised by Mr. Josse. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn next to the 30th session of the Serbian Republic held on September 6, 1992. That needs to be distributed. It is P65, tab 196. And we may as well distribute the next item at the same time, Your Honour, which will need a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1251, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this -- the first document, as indicated, is the 30th session of the Presidency. Present are Dr. Karadzic, Dr. Koljevic, Dr. Plavsic, and you. The item on the agenda is discussion of the proposal for the pardon of prisoners of war held in Manjaca camp, and indicates that the military prosecutor's office has submitted a list of a certain number of prisoners of war held in the Manjaca camp and a proposal for the adoption of a decision that they be spared further criminal prosecution. The Presidency recognised the reasons, it says in the second paragraph, and circumstances of the proposal and adopted the decision to spare the persons named in the list enclosed from criminal prosecution. And if you'll turn to P1251, that's a document of the 1st Krajina Corps command, confidential number 655, dated September 11, 1992. That appears to reflect the list of the 69 persons pardoned or granted amnesty from criminal prosecution. First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, can we confirm that this list of 69 people is the list of prisoners who were pardoned by the Presidency on 6 September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm anything. I don't know. I just see that there was a discussion about this. I don't think that this list was at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it -- does it help to look at the telegram that was received from the Presidency that says, "Pursuant to Article 80 ..." et cetera, et cetera, and then at the conclusion: "At its session held on 6 September, 1992, the Presidency of the Serbian Republic adopted the following decision on granting amnesty for the following prisoners"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but obviously their names are not referred to in the record. A certain number of people were supposed to be pardoned, and they agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, this list is a list of those persons who fell within the category of persons identified by Major Stupar on 20 August, 1992, when he made his introductory remarks about the views of the Presidency, that there should be a list prepared of people against whom there is no evidence that they participated in combat activities and who have serious health conditions and attract the attention of journalists and representatives of humanitarian organisations. That's who these people are. Correct, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. It's the other way around. The prosecutor sent this list to the Presidency, and the Presidency pardoned these people. That is what I see here. I don't know about this list. I just know that this is what was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You didn't know that these were 69 sick people who were held in that camp -- in those camps? That the remaining people who hadn't done anything but weren't sick enough to attract international attention continued to languish in that camp?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I told you what I know. I was present at this meeting that was dealing with the pardon. I was not there. I did not know about their condition. I did not know whether they were sick or not. I didn't know anything about this. This is the document that was there then. I mean, I never looked at it. I never saw it. I didn't know what this was all about. The prosecutor made a proposal to have a certain number of persons pardoned, and they were pardoned by the Presidency. How, how come, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Please turn to the 20th session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one thing? Mr. Krajisnik, did you ask yourself at that time on what basis a certain number of detainees were freed from criminal prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe. I don't know. I'm just telling you that it is only normal that people should be pardoned and released from prison on the basis of a proposal made by the public prosecutor. Maybe I did know at the time, I don't know. I didn't go into the core of the matter at all. They said they should be pardoned. Perhaps all of these arguments were presented there. I don't know, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you say 5.000 people were released by Mr. Karadzic at a certain moment, and suddenly a small number pops up --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it was 500. I know that that's what people said, how many people he released unilaterally. I know there were complaints by deputies that it was no longer possible for us to exchange our people. Because I know that they mentioned a large number. Whether it was just this or whether there was more, I don't know. There was probably more, because this refers just to Manjaca here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And did you see any similar discussions and similar decisions made in the Presidency sessions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only heard the stories they were saying, that there had been a unilateral release and that the Muslim was do the same on the other side, and then they didn't, and some people were angry about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what you told us before. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger. I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, the Chamber is considering whether -- we have taken quite some time from Mr. Tieger this morning, and I noticed that you're reluctantly preparing for starting re-examination. At the same time, we told you yesterday that we would expect you to do so. So therefore I'm a bit hesitant, but we might decide during the break how to proceed this morning. Would you, also in view of what we told you yesterday, which certainly might not have made life easier for you yesterday, would you -- would you oppose under those circumstances if we would allow Mr. Tieger to take the whole of the day and then for you the whole of the Monday, or would you say no, I even prefer that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I certainly wouldn't oppose it, Your Honour. Could I -- could I also make this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: For my part, the more questions that my client is asked by anyone in this courtroom, the better. So if the Court is prepared to grant some extra time, whoever is asking the questions, I, on his behalf, am only too pleased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: All right. Then we'll consider, Mr. Tieger, whether we'll allow you to finish this morning rather than after the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, before you continue --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, before you continue, you more or less suggested that the list of the persons, P1251, would be the same, because you said, "This is a list, a list of those persons who fell within the category of persons identified by Major Stupar on the 20th of August." And a few lines further down, "people against whom there's no evidence that they participated in combat activities and who have serious health conditions and attract the attention of the journalists," which seems to be a reference to the list of 60 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 92, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 92 people. We tried to find on P1251 - we just took the first column, 22 - we find only two out of the first 22 on the other list, that is number 6, then is Gromilic, who is, by the way, not a sick person, who is not described as a sick person but as an underaged person, and number 17, Refik Salihovic, who is, as number 11, on the sick persons list. By the way, another matter is that a list of 92 persons seems to exist of 40 sick people only, which of course raises some additional questions as to the consistency of this document. The Chamber would have appreciated if you would have drawn our attention to these inconsistencies and would like to hear from you whether the remaining 47 on the list, whether we would find a similar outcome if we would compare that with the list of 92, that is that 10 per cent is only on that list of sick people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, here's what I can tell you, Your Honour: Number one, the Court would have heard that, and I think the Court could see how anxious I was to continue with the examination and, with the break, interrupted. Number two, the court is correct, I believe there are three persons on the list of 92 who appear on the list of 69. That's number 6, Mr. Gromilic who you've already indicated, number 17, Mr. Salihovic, and number 29, Dedic. On the list that -- the numbers I'm indicating are on the list of 69.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there's -- the overlap is very limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, the Prosecution's position was not that the list -- that it was the same list but that the category was the same, and I was anxious to proceed with the examination to make that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: They represent -- they reflect the same general category of -- of prisoners; sick and innocent. Your Honour, I haven't finished the examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was at least not clear to us and whether -- what caused the confusion, we'll re-read the transcript in that respect, and please proceed at this moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Has the Chamber decided on the time issue, Your Honour? Could I make one other brief observation which might help --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- and that's this: When we were reviewing the documents that Mr. Krajisnik has submitted over the last few weeks, we remembered the document that he submitted at Your Honour's request at the it end of examination-in-chief and just before cross-examination, that the Chamber, in effect, sent to the CLSS itself for translation. As I understand the position, having liaised with Mr. Aquaviva, who is dealing with the matter, that has not yet come back from the CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the priority list?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The priority list is expected not to arrive not later than Monday morning, and of course the Chamber can't decide on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, that, of course, would help us in our preparations because we might try and incorporate it. It's clearly somewhat -- bearing in mind what Your Honour has said to Mr. Krajisnik about that list, someone needs to deal with it. With respect, either the Court or the Defence. The Prosecution quite obviously are not going to deal with it. So if Your Honour was to say Monday, it would help in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We would agree, Mr. Tieger, to continue today and finish his cross-examination by the end of this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I hope there is no misunderstanding about any intention to convey -- that was my next questions in the list were about the relationship between the list and then moving on to another clarifying point, and it was the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what may have confused us is the transcript, and if you would read specifically 10:27:53, a question which was -- starts approximately at -- 26 minutes past ten up till 28 minutes -- 28, 29 minutes past 10. But please proceed at this moment, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you've heard the comparisons made by both Their Honours and the Prosecution between the list of persons contained in the August 20 or -- meeting - that is tab 306 - which was in at least for the first 42 people, as the Court has indicated, a list of -- a list of persons for whom there is no evidence that they carried out or participated in combat activities and who have serious health problems. Three of those people, as you've heard, appear on the lists of persons who were granted amnesty from criminal prosecution by the Presidency on September 6th, and -- so my question is: Isn't it correct that the list of these 69 people granted amnesty from criminal prosecution on September 6th at that session of the Presidency is a list of people who were both innocent under the terms of the -- that is, people who were known not to have participated in any way in combat activities and people who were known to be sick?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the reason for the amnesty was, but I know from practice that amnesties usually pertain those who are guilty and then they are amnestied. But here there was a proposal from the 1st Krajina Corps and the Presidency did this. I truly cannot recall what the reason for the amnesty was, but I do know that something like that was done at the proposal of the late Mr. Talic. I mean the Krajina Corps. That's what I mean when I say "Talic."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, I'm suggesting to you that in fact you knew very well, and so did many other people, why these people were released from detention, and that was because their condition was such as to attract the attention of the international community. They were sick people who by now the international community was aware of, and releasing at least those people blunted criticism and was an effort to earn some credit with the international community. You knew that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. I only knew that this was done, and I felt it was positive. But what the reason was, I can't recall that. There was some reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn to the 20th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, at page 55 of the English, please, and page 6251 of the B/C/S. That session was held on the 14th and 15th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And given potential page inconsistencies, Your Honour, I want to ensure that the Court has -- that we're on the same page with this. I'm looking now at a portion on page 55 approximately nine lines down from the top, a sentence that begins in the middle of the page, "About the prisoners of war ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that we have the minutes and not -- we've got here the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We will provide -- and again, I really -- okay. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may well be -- do you know -- it's submitted under what number?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this -- my best recollection is when the Court asked whether it had all the sessions from 1991 and 1992, we indicated that all of them were being provided. This was the last one provided because it was the last one we received, and so I think in the original materials the Court did not have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then we received it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we were not able to bring every day everything --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we were provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But we have a copy here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is an exhibit number, I could get it on my screen, hopefully. That would be 20th. Yes, this is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I think we discussed this the other day. It was the one we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you take us to page --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 55, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 55, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: About the ninth line down from the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Tieger, the exhibit number, was that assigned?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think we agreed that that should be done. I don't remember that it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, do you remember whether we did? If not, then we'll provisionally then assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1252, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1252. I do everything with pencil, so -- we'll check whether this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That section begins -- Mr. Krajisnik, I see you've been reading that section, so I'm confident that you're familiar with it now, but just in case you haven't located it, it is toward the bottom half of page 6251 in the B/C/S, and it states -- this is Dr. Karadzic speaking, saying the following: "About the prisoners of war, about three weeks before they started talking about the camps, we submitted a 16-page pamphlet to the British parliament to all important foreign correspondents about concentration camps for Serbs but no one paid any attention. We must know that we have to act like whores and talk to foreign journalists. We cannot not reply when the foreign journalists call either Nikola or me and talk to them, waste our time with them. But despite all that, we have to do the elementary things. We cannot let up regarding the elementary things. The army will not let up, and neither will we by not asking the army. Disbanding Trnopolje does not mean letting up. If they want to take them abroad, let them. If they want to take 69 sick people tomorrow, let them. That will give us great credit among the international public. We want to cooperate. We want to deal with humanitarian issues, and that helps us. Don't worry about that. We don't need Manjaca. If only all the Green Berets had been killed with a rifle in their hand, but once they've been captured, then we must abide by the Geneva Conventions and it's all for nothing. It would suit us if it were shut down, disbanded, shut down and sent somewhere, but not for them to return to the battlefield." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, Dr. Karadzic's reference to the 69 sick people whom the international community wanted, that was a reference to the 69 people on the Presidency list who were granted amnesty on September 6th, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe the Red Cross visited them and established that they were sick and drew up a list and the prosecutor decided they should be released. That was the route to be followed. Somebody had to establish that they were ill. Maybe that was done in prison. But it's not innocent people who are amnestied. It's only those who are guilty. If we're talking about an amnesty, if they were innocent then the prosecutor should have released them immediately. The prosecutor and the judges have the right to release them. The army could have released them without the Presidency. I'm just interpreting here. I remember that there were objections made to Mr. Karadzic, and he responded that all prisons should be disbanded, that we have no use for them. I don't know where I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. He also responded by telling the deputies, "Don't worry about it. We're sending them out of here, and that's good."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If they're fit for military service and if they want to go abroad rather than return to their territory, that was a plus, otherwise they would take up their rifles and fight against us. As they have decided to go abroad, he says that's a good thing. It's better than them going back there and fighting against us. It doesn't mean that the international -- that had the International Red Cross wanted them to go to Bosnia they wouldn't have released them, because those who were released were arrested again two or three times, maybe two times. You release someone and he goes to their territory and then he fights again with a rifle in his hand. That's how it was when there were exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you have any idea why these 69 sick people, and many, many others, of course, wanted to go abroad rather than returning home?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. It was the Ministry of Health are that issued an order to the MUP. They probably established that these people were ill. I don't know why this was agreed, but there must have been a reason. If they were ill, they had to be released so they could be treated, or I don't know. They shouldn't have been detained at all, if I may say that. They should have received medical treatment. I don't know how.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what were the elementary things that Dr. Karadzic assured the deputies that the leadership and the army would not give up on?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the way I interpret it, what is meant is, and as a reference to the conference above this, we have to worry about the elementary things, don't worry about these people, because the deputies were saying they'll go back there and fight against us again. So elementary things, that doesn't refer to the prisoners, it refers to negotiations, defence lines, demarcation lines; those things. I remember when he said that prisons should be disbanded, and you see he mentions Manjaca here and Trnopolje. So probably that's what happened, I don't know, but it was about this time that it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turn to tab 315, please. That's P892, tab 99. This is a report from the 1st Krajina Corps command to the Republika Srpska army Main Staff on December 16, 1992. Item number 3, situation on the territory: "1001 prisoners were released today from the Manjaca camp. They were escorted out of the RS territory. 413 of them still remain, scheduled to be released on Friday, 18 December, 1992. There have been no other significant changes." Were new prisoners brought into Manjaca between what you said was around this time, between mid-September, 1992, or did the same prisoners who were there at the time of the Assembly session we just looked at continue to languish in Manjaca until the time of the 1 KK report?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what prisoners this is about. I can only add that in many prisons there were prisoners who were there for four years on both sides. If they were released in late 1992, then compared to others, that's good, but I don't know what this is about. I have to say I don't know what prisoners this refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Could you turn, please, to tab 317.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That needs a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1253, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
