utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Hamdija Suhonjic was the first person on the list of those granted amnesty from criminal prosecution on September 6 by the Presidency, and indeed as -- well, I mean, first I should say that P1253, for identification, is a May 31, 1993, article from the Guardian that focuses in part on Mr. Suhonjic. Mr. Suhonjic, as the article indicates, who was in his 60s, was a carpenter. He describes his arrest. He indicates on page 2 of the B/C/S and the top of page 2 in the English that by the time he was rescued from a third camp, Manjaca, he was suffering from starvation and dysentery and had lost 40 pounds, and on September 15th was identified, was -- he attracted, I guess, the attention of the international community, who saw him, as it says here, "one of 68 inmates of Manjaca in need of urgent medical treatment." And he was taken to Britain, as the article indicates, for that emergency care. If you would turn to one more tab, tab 311.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That needs a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1254, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P1254 is an article from the Houston Chronicle from October --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you happen to have it in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's coming to you. The article begins by describing Omarska and then the treatment of the prisoners in Manjaca, indicating that thousands packed the offices, workshops, and storage rooms and the hangar and glass and brick administration building. All were on starvation diets. That's on the first page. And then if we continue down to the bottom of page 2, after a description of the general fate of many of the detainees, including beatings, executions, disease and starvation, we see a reference to Mr. Edin Elkaz, who is number 3 on the list. His name is found at the very bottom of the second page, which is -- the last four digits of which are 7471. "900 miles from here outside London" the article states, "Edin Elkaz lies awake nights, his head filled with the screams of the men being tortured in the room next door in the white house." On the next page the document indicates that interviews had been conducted of the 68 people taken to Britain to recover from beatings and shootings, Mr. Elkaz being one of them, Mr. Elkaz appearing as number 3 on the list of the 69 persons granted amnesty by the Presidency on September 6th. Those people we've mentioned, Mr. Krajisnik, were obviously just a fraction of the people and the experiences on the list of those who were released by the Presidency on September 6th for the reasons described by Dr. Karadzic at the 20th session. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What it says in the minutes, that more people were released in addition to these 60.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 68, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. We've had an opportunity to look at and ask you questions about the extent of the investigations conducted into the reasons why people were in camps, their treatment in camps, and the responsibility of these who were in direct contact with those prisoners and detainees. I just want to look at two more documents in connection with that. You earlier referred to Simo Drljaca, and before we took a look at some of the documentation concerning Omarska, you referred to him as the person who essentially ran a secret camp in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. I don't know when I said he ran a secret camp. What I said was that he reported that there was no camp in Prijedor. I didn't have any knowledge about him running a camp. I don't know when I said that he was running a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There's no question, is there, that Simo Drljaca was the chief of police and in charge of the police forces that operated or participated in the operation of the Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje camps; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Simo Drljaca was the chief of police in Prijedor, and if the police was securing - and I saw from the documents that they were - then he was in charge of them. That's my reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What investigative efforts were made, to your knowledge, to identify the criminal responsibility of Simo Drljaca for the fate of those thousands of people who passed through, some many of whom did not make it out, of Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje? How was Mr. Drljaca treated for his responsibility for Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje by the Bosnian Serb authorities, by the Bosnian Serb leadership? Tell the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no knowledge of what his role was, but I can tell you what happened to him. He was replaced by the minister and transferred to Bijeljina. Why, I don't know. And I know that later on he was an inspector in the MUP. I did not know what he was doing. This was within the competence of the minister. Well, later on he was killed, but that is not relevant to your question. There is a report here where he complains that there are some disagreements with the civilian authorities in Prijedor and that they are to be blamed for his removal. I read that in some report. When I came here, that's where I read the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to distribute the next item, which is an article in Kozarski Vjesnik, P752D.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, this article I have read, yes. I mean, I glanced at it, I skimmed through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. This is not the item I identified. This item apparently needs a number. It is an article from Kozarski Vjesnik of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1255, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As indicated, Mr. Krajisnik, P1255 is an article from Kozarski Vjesnik of 9 April, 1993, with Simo Drljaca, by then the assistant minister of the interior of the Republika Srpska. And if we look quickly at page 2 of the English, the last paragraph before the subheading on that page, "A huge job done. Assistant Minister Drljaca reflects upon and identifies the number of interviews conducted in the Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje collection centres."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you find it, Mr. Krajisnik? It's the left column.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "A huge job was done." Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just above that, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You found reference to Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje, and the number 6.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then he continues: "Instead of meting out just punishment to them, the world powers forced us to release them all from Manjaca." Now, two things, Mr. Krajisnik, two questions about that article. Number one, it reflects that by April of 1993, Mr. Drljaca had received a promotion to the position of assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was formally so, but you see here, it says that he was removed and that he's embittered by that. I did not know that that was the case. I thought that he was some kind of official, an inspector, but I see here he was assistant minister. I know that he was an insignificant personality. He -- well, what mattered to him was that he lost power, and that matters to all policemen. I mean, really, I haven't seen this before. That's the title he had, but he was so bitter because he had been removed. And why these disagreements took place, well, as I said, I just scanned the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's look at one more document, then, concerning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you say that he was bitter. Do you know what happened to him after he had been assistant minister? Do you know his further career of Mr. Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I know that he was replaced. Later, at some point in time, he was removed from the police. I know that he was demobilised. I know that an arrest warrant was issued, an indictment was issued against him, and he was killed during the arrest. But I did not follow --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We've been trying to find out, Your Honour - because we've worked out he was indicted here - if my learned friend could inform certainly the Defence and perhaps the Chamber what happened to those proceedings. We're quite anxious to know. We've been unable to find out on the website, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what happened to Mr. Drljaca, it was in the newspapers, I think that when -- I think there was an attempt to arrest him in the Prijedor area by foreign military and that this resulted in an exchange of fire in which Mr. Drljaca died.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what my general knowledge is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Presumably that's what Mr. Krajisnik was just alluding to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that he was referring to that. And I remember reading it in the newspaper, that it was -- I was on holiday, I remember that, so therefore it must have been somewhere in August, I don't know which --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, in your responses concerning Mr. Drljaca's subsequent positions, are you trying to suggest that the Bosnian Serb leadership disapproved of what he and his subordinates had done in Prijedor and in Omarska and Keraterm and Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know why he was removed, and no one knew about it. This is the line of work of the minister. They probably had some reasons. He is saying here that there was a disagreement between him and the municipal authorities, as far as I can see here. I don't have any other knowledge. There was some kind of problem, and that is why he was removed, replaced. Somebody had asked for that. I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the fact is that Prijedor, which had once had over 49.000 Muslims in it, was violently cleansed by, among other military forces, the police under the direction of Mr. Drljaca. Muslims were rounded up and placed in Keraterm, Omarska, and Trnopolje and mistreated in the manner we've seen in that article, and Mr. Drljaca and numbers of his subordinates received awards from the Republika Srpska leadership for those efforts. Isn't that the fact?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he received any awards, but if he did receive a decoration, then a proposal was made to that effect, and that falls under the jurisdiction of the Presidency or, rather, the president of the republic. If that is so, well, many people got decorations. But I don't think it was on account of torturing the Muslims. Probably because of a description stating that he fought for Prijedor or something like that. He certainly would not have been decorated if people knew that he had killed, tortured Muslims, and so on. I'm convinced that no one would ever have done such a thing. There is a commission for decorations that receives these proposals, then presents proposals to Karadzic, and then he confers a decoration upon someone.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that article relates a large ceremony in Prijedor attended by, among others, General Major Subotic. And, as we can see further on down the page, an award was bestowed by Dr. Karadzic. In the speech before the -- apparently before the awards were bestowed, they -- Bogdan Delic talked about, among other things, "The taking over of power and the attack on Prijedor, the events that followed and the participation of the members of the police in military operations in Republika Srpska and Srpska Krajina, for which they were thanked under decorations. The President of Republika Srpska, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, awarded the medal Petar Mrkonjic to the police station in Prijedor and the Karadjordje Star medal to the former head and now assistant in the Ministry of the Interior, Simo Drljaca." Dusan Jankovic, the Prijedor Police Station assistant; Milutin Cadjo, commander; and Miroslav Paras, all of whom we heard about during the course of this case, also received awards. By 26th of November, 1993, Mr. Krajisnik, much of the world, if not the entire world, knew what had happened in Omarska from a variety of sources. Isn't it the case that Dr. Karadzic bestowed this award on Drljaca and his subordinates and, just as was indicated earlier in the article, for their efforts in Prijedor, including Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje through which the Muslim -- many, many, many members of the Muslim community passed before they were sent out of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm convinced that the commission for decorations and the responsible people in the republic did not know about what was learned about later. Had they known at the time what had happened in Prijedor, if these people are guilty, they would not have bestowed decorations upon them. As for the writings of foreign journalists, I told you about what this same Kozarski Vjesnik wrote and what people who visited the prisons said. I am not challenging that this happened, but at this time when the decorations were being given, I'm convinced that no one would have been awarded for committing crimes. Probably they didn't even know about this. Rather, they were decorated for the liberation of Prijedor, and they said that the police did that without a single shot being fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What about you, Mr. Krajisnik? When do you say that you learned about the atrocities in Omarska, about the treatment of the Muslims and Croats in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, when I came here I learned of many things that I had never known. I did not know about these crimes in Prijedor. When I was a member of the Presidency, delegations came to see me. A delegation a people from Prijedor who were indicted. They were saying, "We're not guilty. Somebody's indicting us." And I even made an effort for this being established. I attended the funeral of Mr. Drljaca, and I did not know that he was involved in that. Had I known, I mean, would I go to the funeral of someone who had killed people, and would I go to express my condolences? Crimes were being concealed terribly, and they are revealed only later when peace is established. Can you have a look at the first article? Mr. Drljaca says, "When we establish rule of law, things will be known that are unknown now." I saw that in the first article. He himself is saying that. No one was bragging about war crimes. Everybody was hiding them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Unless the Court has some additional questions, I'm going to -- I need, in light of the time, to move on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we briefly go into private session, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, the -- please proceed. I think we need still a number for the document you referred to in your last question. Is that -- last series of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that would have been the last series.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's Kozarski Vjesnik, 26 November, 1993. Mr. Registrar that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1256, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, over the course of your examination-in-chief, you were asked on a number of occasions about aspects of the War Presidency or expanded Presidency, and on May 19th, for example, you -- as a general matter, of course, as you said on May 25th, the expanded Presidency or War Presidency -- you said that the state of war was never declared and there was never an expanded Presidency, and as you explained in somewhat more detail on May 19th, referring to the document establishing War Presidencies, you indicated that that decision had no foundation in the constitutional law and was wrong in the way it was formulated. You said, "The expansion of the Presidency was not something that was supposed to be done in case of an immediate threat of war, only the state of war, but in doing this they must have been assuming -- they must have been thinking that they were going to introduce the state of war. However, that didn't occur and so those War Presidencies were abolished very soon." And as I understood you, that was -- you were explaining that it was quickly recognised that there was no basis for the establishment of War Presidencies and so the War Presidencies were very quickly abolished soon after their enactment at the beginning of June. Now, Mr. Krajisnik, in that connection I'd like to quickly run through a few documents before moving on. I think we need to have additional documents distributed, Your Honour, for that purpose. Let me check the bundle. They have been distributed? All right. Spare me a moment. Can we turn first to tab 327. That's P64, P65, tab 144, and P529, tab 111. Also P1109. Just very quickly, Mr. Krajisnik. This is the law on amending the constitutional law for implementing the constitution. It states in Article 1: "During state of war, the Presidency is expanded with the following members: The president of the National Assembly and the Prime Minister of the government of the Serb Republic." It indicates also that after paragraph 5 new paragraphs 6 and 7 are added and read: "During a state of war, the Presidency may decide to establish War Presidencies in the municipalities." And looking quickly at tab 324. P64, P65, tab 142. That's the decision by the Presidency on the adoption by the Presidency of the decision on the establishment of War Presidencies in municipalities during war or imminent threat of war. That's from 31 May, 1992. And then quickly in -- at tab 325 we can see the decision. P64, P65, tab 143. P529, tab 110. And that states: "Pursuant to Article 5, paragraphs 6 and 7 of the constitutional law on implementing the constitution, decision on the formation of War Presidencies in municipalities in times of war or the immediate threat of war." And in Article 3 we can see what the War Presidencies were about; organising, coordinating, adjusting activities, et cetera. In Article 4 we see the responsibilities of the Republic's representative, to ensure permanent coordination, as it states at the top of the page in English on 9978. Now, Mr. Krajisnik, you've already brought our attention to the difference between, and that -- the state of war as it appears in -- at tab 327 in the law on amending the constitutional law, and the Presidency minutes of 31 May we've just looked at, and the decision on formation of the War Presidencies. In fact, that was a distinction that was brought to the Court's attention, to the best of my recollection, early on in the Prosecution case as well. So those are the decisions and the law to which you were referring in the portion of your testimony that I read out earlier; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the decision was reached autonomously by the Presidency of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, it does not pertain to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you referring to other decisions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to tell you that the decision was reached before the constitutional law, on the 31st, and the constitutional law was on the 2nd and the 1st and it was up before the Presidency. This constitutional law was not at the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Tieger only asked you whether the decisions he just mentioned and the law, that these are the documents you were referring to in the portion of your testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, yes. Yes, yes, yes. These are documents that I was actually referring to. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then you pointed out that -- or you testified that everyone quickly became aware of -- well, a state of war wasn't declared and that the War Presidencies were then abolished as a result of that, and that indicates that there were no War Presidencies and there was no republic War Presidency either. That's what I understood you to say. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that we knew then that this was an unlawful decision. It was replaced on the 10th of June with a war commissioner, and that's when the War Presidency was abolished. That is to say the decision was replaced before it entered into force with a municipal commissioner, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So are you saying that everybody at the time believed that the establishment of War Presidencies was lawful?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. We didn't even give it any thought. This was a decision that was proposed by the government directly to the Presidency, and we adopted it. It doesn't say there on the basis of which constitutional law this is being done at the Presidency, it's just stated that a decision was reached. You have that in the government records that this decision was being reached, not on the basis of what.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the decision to establish War Presidencies in the municipality -- in the municipalities was based on the same law on amending the constitutional law for implementing the constitution that the establishment of the republic War Presidency was based on; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Please. This was adopted autonomously. The government proposed it to the Presidency. We didn't know pursuant to what it would be done. And these two decisions are treated separately. Later on, when they formulated the decision, they wrote down pursuant to what, but this was before the constitutional law was passed, the 2nd of June, whereas this was on the 31st of May. And Mrs. Plavsic gave instructions on the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sure -- I think it's going to be helpful, then, to look at what happened after that, including the establishment of commissioners, as you've just mentioned. So why don't we look next at tab 329. By the way, before we go there, I think the interpreters recognise this distinction, but I am told that the term in B/C/S for commission and commissioners in this context is "povjerenistvo," and, commissioner "povjerenik," rather than "komisija" or something of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From nodding, I see that this is confirmed by the interpreters, and interpreted half way. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tab 329 is P64, P65, tab 157. That's a decision by the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of BH held during an imminent threat of war on 10 June, 1992. And item number 8 reflects the decision on the establishment of War Commissions in the municipalities during war or an imminent threat of war or in the state of war. And as we see further on down in that session, the list of commissioners was compiled and the persons indicated were appointed commissioners. And if we could then look next at the decision on establishing War Commissions at tab 330. That's P64A, P529, tab 112. Now, first of all, Mr. Krajisnik, looking at the very top of the page, it states: "Pursuant to Article 5, paragraphs 6 and 7 of the constitutional law on the implementation of the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," those are the same provisions we have seen -- we saw just a moment ago in the law on implementing -- on amending the constitutional law and in the official decision on formation of the War Presidencies. So let's read on down the page. "The decision on the establishment of War Commissions in municipalities in time of imminent threat of war or during a state of war." And in that decision, Mr. Krajisnik, you will see three separate references to the existence of the War Presidency of the Republic, that is the Republic war -- the war -- the Republic War Presidency. In Article 3, it states: "War Commissions shall maintain the closest possible cooperation with the legal authorities. They shall convey directives issued by the War Presidency of the Republic." In Article 4, beginning at the send sentence: "State commissioners shall appoint the War Presidencies in consultation with the War Presidency of the Republic." Next sentence: "State commissioners shall dissolve the municipal War Presidencies and appoint new members in consultation with the War Presidency of the Republic." Now, this decision, Mr. Krajisnik, is the one that abolished or rescinded or superseded the War Presidencies, replacing them with war commissioners; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Abolishing War Presidencies and establishing War Commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was based on the same amendment to the constitutional law that established the War Presidencies in the first place and that also established the Republic War Presidency, the one that's found at tab 327.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republican War Presidency was not formed pursuant to these amendments. This is wrong. It could only have been done during the state of war. Take a look and you'll see. It's quite clear. There is not a War Presidency anywhere. It is just that the Presidency is being extended. However, the term "War Presidency" is not used in -- in here, of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is not used in where; in the decision on the establishment of War Commissions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the law. In the law. It's not used in the war, the term "the War Presidency of Republika Srpska." It's only said that the Presidency is being extended.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During a state of war the War Presidency is extended, thereby becoming, colloquially, a War Presidency. No?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It becomes the Presidency. The Presidency. There is no War Presidency mentioned here. It would have been called the War Presidency. It only says the Presidency is being extended, and it bears the name of Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. And before we move on, let's just take a look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just ask you a question. Mr. Krajisnik, we have gone through most of this problem five if not 10 times. Now, Mr. Karadzic signs a decision in which that functioning of War Commissions is established, and several times reference is made to the War Presidency of the Republic. Now, you say it's not under law, so it isn't there. At least Mr. Karadzic, at the time he signed this, he issued this, at least he must have been under the impression that such a thing did exist, and -- so therefore do you have a solution for that? I mean, in the thinking of those who drafted this, who signed this, there must have been a -- well, an idea that such a thing did exist. And you said, well, it's contrary to the law, that's more or less to say, because the law is talking about an expanded Presidency, so it couldn't be there. But in real life it seems that it was on paper there, although conflicting legal instance, and it may have been in the minds of persons as well. So just to sum up, it's contrary to the law, so your testimony sounds as if the matter has been resolved by that answer. Couldn't exist contrary to the law, therefore it didn't exist. Could you comment on, or at least give your views on --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- perhaps on the issue I raised, not to repeat that the terminology was not exactly what you find in the law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This proposal was made by Mr. Djokanovic for Mr. Karadzic to sign, and he testified about this. In the decision we heard at the Presidency, it was only municipal commissions that were established. Not a single meeting of that Presidency was in wartime or as a War Presidency. It was only a Presidency during an imminent threat of war. Had Karadzic known this, he would have referred to it as a meeting of the War Presidency later on, but they were all meetings during an imminent threat of war. There is not one except when the military were there. This is a decision which was written down which I didn't look at. There was a decision about commissioners. What the form was, well, somebody wrote it down, but it couldn't have been that the War Presidency was established, it was only a Presidency pursuant to the law. But it was Mr. Djokanovic -- well, he may have thought there was a War Presidency, what do I know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You limit the awareness to Mr. Djokanovic. You said you -- or you didn't read this, and therefore -- well, I leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if this exists in one person's mind who writes it down, and then if it's contrary to the law, you say, well, it wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. President, it wasn't important to me what the form was if there was a war. I learnt here that it was he who wrote that decision. I never read it. Perhaps I knew that commissioners existed, but now I see this could not have been established pursuant to that law. Only municipal presidencies could have been established in wartime. These articles were not for the commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I intend to get into some contemporaneous accounts of -- of the understanding of the situation, so that may help and I indicated that to the Court if it had any questions. Could I ask -- I'm grateful for the additional time, but might I ask for a slightly shorter than usual break so we could reassemble and maximise my -- nothing out of the ordinary, but just if we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say -- it's a very kind way of saying, Mr. Tieger, that 20 minutes is 20 minutes. Let 20 minutes be 20 minutes today. That is we will resume at 12.50 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we just looked at the provisions, the conditions and provisions giving rise to the -- to a Republican War Presidency, war -- municipal War Presidencies, and municipal War Commissions, and I indicated to the Court that we would turn to the contemporaneous understandings of what was occurring with respect to the existence of a War Presidency. We've already seen, for example, during the course of this case Mr. Subotic's remarks at the 19th session on 12 August, his complaint that he's probably the only Defence Minister in the world who is not a member of the War Presidency of the Republic, and also Mr. Bijelic's comment -- that's at page 58 of the English, Your Honour. And also Mr. Bijelic's comment that -- shortly thereafter, that, "However, at this moment when we have the army, when we have the War Presidency, my question is who needs paramilitaries? Whose are those paramilitaries?" Et cetera. But I wanted to take you in particular to a session at which this issue was discussed at -- was focused on and discussed at some length, and that is the 22nd session of the RS Assembly, held in November of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the benefit of the Court, that can be found at tab 345, I believe. It's P65, Treanor 14, tab 213. So that I think in this instance we'll have -- all have the same version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 345 seems to be the 22nd session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did I not say the 22nd, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least it appears on the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 22nd, Your Honour, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And let's turn first to the remarks of Mr. Trbojevic at page 49 of the English and page 9680 of the B/C/S. And, Mr. Krajisnik, those remarks that I will be focusing on begin at the bottom of page 9679 and continue on to the top of 9680.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the remarks are contained at the beginning of what would be essentially the third paragraph, which begins, "The third aspect ..." on page 49.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm looking at the second sentence now, or the third sentence. "First of all, we have a parallel system of authority. The public and 'legal' wartime Presidency is an organ of authority that isn't mentioned in the constitution. Wartime commissioners working in the field are neither recognised by the constitution nor the law. What this means is that from the top of the state down to the level of municipality, there is parallel system of authority."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find it on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Which page are you on, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this here, 680 you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I said it starts at the bottom of page 9679 and continues on to the top of 9680.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... fourth line from the bottom. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, at pages 58 through 59 of the English -- well, let's just move straight on. Let's turn to Dr. Karadzic at page 60 of the English and page 9691 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At the bottom of page 60 of the English and page 9691 of the B/C/S, Dr. Karadzic addresses himself to that issue, and I can turn you -- before I move on to that, Mr. Krajisnik, I can turn you to some other comments in the session at which at least one other deputy raises the question of whether there should be any Presidency at all, which he refers to as a rudiment of communism. So by the time Dr. Karadzic speaks - he speaks shortly before Dr. Karadzic - two questions are on the table; the one raised by Mr. Trbojevic, the legality of the wartime Presidency and the commissioners, and the one raised by Mr. Bosiljcic about whether there should be any Presidency at all, instead just have a president rather than a communist artefact of a collective body. And then Mr. Karadzic speaks at the bottom of page 60: "I was always on the side of the Presidency, not the president. There are only a few of us as it is. If Koljevic and I go somewhere, then Biljana stays. At least there is one of the three of us. But if Biljana leaves, then Mr. Krajisnik. But we receive calls from 50 different places. We are overextended." And then, Mr. Krajisnik, at page 100 of the English, after some period of time goes on and some inquiry has been made on this subject, you speak. That's at page 9729 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 9729 are the last four digits of that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this starts, Your Honour, at the first full paragraph after the declaration of the appointment of a public prosecutor in Krupa Na Uni. Mr. Krajisnik states: "Gentlemen, we have received a response to the deputy question on wartime Presidency and commissioners. The question was raised by Mr. Trbojevic and it has been clearly stated that this isn't compliant with the constitution. It should be forwarded to the constitutional committee if we decide that we need to have a wartime Presidency and commissioners. If we don't opt for that, this has to be an initiative and it doesn't need to be sent to the --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apologies, can you give us a precise reference, please, in the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik's got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand the problem. I'm sorry about that. It's -- let me see. Correct. That portion begins on 9728, I believe. If you see the reference to Krupa Na Uni, just above the last two paragraphs, that's where that section begins. "Gentlemen, we have received a response ..." Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So, Mr. Krajisnik, here you indicate that you've received a response to the question on wartime Presidency and commissioners raised by Mr. Trbojevic, stating that it isn't compliant with the constitution and should be forwarded to the constitutional committee if there is a decision to keep the wartime Presidency, and the decision that we need to have this wartime Presidency and commissioners, and if we don't decide to have it, then there'll need to be an initiative for that but it won't have to be sent to the constitutional committee. Then you say: "I hereby open the discussion first, or if we need to vote, if discussion isn't necessary, but we first need to decide whether or not we need a wartime Presidency and commissioners. If we do, then we should send the initiative to the constitutional committee so that it can prepare changes to the constitution and that they can be incorporated." Then a little further on, after a quick departure to discuss the editor-in-chief of Serbian Voice, you say: "We now move on to the Assembly's position on whether or not we need a wartime Presidency. Wartime Presidency consists of three members of the Presidency, the president of the National Assembly and the Prime Minister. Since a state of war haven't been declared, this is deemed unconstitutional, as is the appointment of commissioners. I hereby open the discussion. Who wants the floor? Please, we are dealing with the wartime Presidency of the Republic and the commissioners. Are commissioners appointed by the state, in other words, deputies? Does anyone have anything to discuss? No. Let us decide, please. Do we need to change the constitution to include that wartime Presidency will be formed during a declared immediate threat of war or a declared state of war? Who is in favour? Who is opposed?" You give the floor to someone "since we haven't voted yet." And you indicate, "We are now discussing whether or not we need a wartime Presidency without stating who will perform the function." So apparently the question that can be heard from the benches is about who will be on it. "We are now discussing whether or not we need a wartime Presidency without stating who will perform the function. That's how it's been so far. Now we need to incorporate it into the constitution. We need to have this initiative to have a minister of defence." Again a reflection of Subotic's interest in being on the wartime Presidency. "Who will perform this function? Let's not decide this now. We should definitely have a wartime Presidency during an immediate threat of war whereas the members of wartime Presidency will be nominated by the constitutional committee. We don't need to vote again. Let us decide on commissioners. The opinion here is that we need commissioners in Republika Srpska." And just a couple of additional comments made during that session, Mr. Krajisnik, first by Mr. Maksimovic at page 103 of the English and page 9732 of the B/C/S, found at the very -- beginning -- it's the beginning of the Mr. Maksimovic's remarks but it's the last three lines of the page in English on 103: "Sometime at the end of May or beginning of June, following a decision issued by our wartime Presidency, wartime commissioners were established for certain regions and deputies were tasked with that duty." And then at the end of his remarks, found at the bottom of page 104 of the English and the very top of 105, Mr. Maksimovic says, after describing some of his experiences, having been tasked: "This is some of my experience: I don't think this should be a permanent or constant institution. I think that only the wartime Presidency should decide about numbers and the people, that the wartime Presidency alone should assess which areas need deputies it. It should be good for them to rotate frequently, not to remain in one place for long but move on for the exact reasons Mr. President already mentioned." And immediately thereafter we see Mr. Djokanovic addressing everyone assembled, who says, "I am one of those who participated in the creation of the concept of commissioners and their work and the establishment of commissioners' offices and I think I was one of the first commissioners of the wartime Presidency of Republika Srpska." His comments go -- continue, talking about his task as was that of Mr. Maksimovic, and then he states, about a dozen lines up from the bottom, after listing the municipalities in which he served as a commissioner: "Now the wartime Presidency should, if the Assembly decides to keep commissioners, make a selection and exactly determine which municipalities commissioners need to visit, because the function of civilian organs of authority has now been restored and commissioners can now concentrate on their part of the job, because in my opinion they really completed the part of the job that was necessary at that moment." Now, those remarks, Mr. Krajisnik, are a reflection of the uniform understanding of all of those assembled; members of the Bosnian Serb leadership, the deputies, that there was a wartime Presidency consisting, as you said, of the three members of the collective Presidency, the Prime Minister and the president of the Assembly, that it turns out not to comply, as Trbojevic pointed out, with the technicalities of the law, and so there was a decision made whether to keep it and change the constitution so that it would comply or to have an initiative and discard it.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, everything you have read out goes to support the fact that there was no extended Presidency. I will only remind you that Mr. Trbojevic complained about a three-member Presidency because it is not there in the constitution. There is only the president of the Republic. There were two legal members of the Presidency and one illegal one, and that was Mr. Karadzic, and that was what he meant when he said extended Presidency. Let me remind you of Mr. Karadzic's statement that you read out here. He says, "When I'm not there, Koljevic is there. When Koljevic isn't there, Plavsic is there. One of the three of us." Then there is a comma, "and if Plavsic is not there, Krajisnik is there." Why didn't he say Mr. Djeric is there too if the extended Presidency existed? In order to save time, I will tell you there is an Assembly decision on abolishing the Presidency or, rather, the municipal Presidencies. Had there been a Republic Presidency, there would have been a decision on abolishing the Republic extend Presidency, but, however, it was only the municipal Presidency that was abolished because those were the only ones that existed. And you can have a look at that. It was in November, 1992. There would have been a Presidency. It wouldn't have been implied. At that time, people called everything wartime and Serbian. The commission looked into the fact -- into whether we needed a Presidency, and they concluded that it could not be done now. Had -- so the constitution was changed, the Presidency was abolished, and the president of the Republic was established at the end of the year. It was not an extended Presidency that was established. People were against a three-member Presidency. They wanted a single person, and then those two were appointed deputy presidents. And Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Djeric remained at the positions they had held up to that point. This does not show that there was a War Presidency. It's another matter when people use that word because there was a war going on, so they called it a War Presidency. However, in the law it says Presidency, not War Presidency. I may have said War Presidency myself sometimes, but that doesn't mean that it was based on this law. I would have known if I had been a member of the Presidency. I would have signed my name or I would have said that I was a member of the Presidency, but you find a single document which I signed as a member of the Presidency. It can't be that I was the only person who didn't know I was a member of the Presidency and that everybody else knew. I never used the authorities of president. I never signed any decisions as such or punished anyone or did anything else in that capacity. I only attended meetings, just as some other people were present at those meetings from the government and Assembly and so on, and that's the truth. According to this, the Presidency had a session and the Assembly had a session after that, and there was a decision on abolishing the municipal commissions because it had been an unconstitutional decision.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Krajisnik please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn next, Mr. Krajisnik, to tab 344, the minutes of the 22nd session of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The minutes of that same session, that needs a number Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1257, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P1257, as indicated, are the minutes of the 22nd session. Let's turn, please, to the last page, item 39, which states: "There was a wide-ranging debate on a question posed by a delegate at the last session of the Assembly concerning whether the formation of a War Presidency and commission was in line with the constitution. Various opinions were expressed on whether the existence of the commission and its activities were justifiable. After the discussion, it was concluded that the Republican Presidency should thoroughly investigate the justification for the existence of the War Presidency and submit its position to the Assembly constitutional commission. The constitutional commission will examine all aspects of this question and submit a specific proposal to the Assembly." And it is signed and stamped -- stamped, and then it is signed by you, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did sign this. And this explains what I've just said. I don't know how it's been translated, but you have a decision pursuant to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Regarding the justification for the existence of the War Presidency, as it says in the last paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, give me the session of the Presidency, please, and you'll see exactly what the standpoint taken by the Presidency was. About establishing a War Presidency, that's what this is about. It was a decision as to whether a War Presidency existed or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, before we turn to other documents, you said this just supports what I just said. I cannot follow you yet, because item 39 explains that the discussion was about the formation of a War Presidency and commission was in line with the constitution, and then it says that it should be thoroughly investigated. Well, the justification for the existence of the War Presidency should be thoroughly investigated. I -- I can't follow you if you say, "This is exactly what I said, what this supports," because it very much looks as if the existing War Presidency is deemed to be not in accordance with the constitution, and that's not what I remember you told us. You said it didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it didn't exist. That's right. I will just read -- the forming of a War Presidency was not according to the constitution. It couldn't be established according to the constitution. You can see there's a decision about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether there's a decision about that. "Concerning whether," as it reads in English, "the formation of a War Presidency and commission was in line with the constitution." It says "was in line with the constitution," not whether the formation of a War Presidency would be in line or is in line with the constitution, at least in the translation, but perhaps we have to look at that very carefully. It says, "was in line," which suggests that the War Presidency --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not what it says here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we should perhaps very carefully look at what it says in the B/C/S. But in the second portion, it says "to investigate the justification for the existence of the War Presidency." It doesn't say to investigate the justification to form a War Presidency, or -- it says "for the existence." But if you say there's a translation problem, I think it's important enough to have this portion of this -- to be reviewed very carefully.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just read what I mean? "After a discussion, it was concluded that the Presidency of the Republic -" so the Presidency, not the War Presidency - "should thoroughly investigate the justification for the existence of the War Presidency." So had a War Presidency existed, it would have said here that the War Presidency should thoroughly investigate the justification for the existence of the War Presidency. That's why I said it supports what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, Mr. Krajisnik, it speaks about the existence of the War Presidency should be investigated, not the formation --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't know how it reads in English, but it says here that there was a whole discussion about the justification for the existence of the War Presidency, and the conclusion that was reached was that it should not exist, and you can see the constitution. So the constitution was not to be changed in order to introduce a War Presidency, because that's what would have had to be done. The establishing of a War Presidency would have been unconstitutional. So only the commissions were abolished. The War Presidency was not abolished because it didn't exist. There's a decision about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. I don't want to deflect the Court from this document but maybe the next document will be of some assistance in that regard as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to tab 346. That's P64, P65, tab 214. The minutes of the session of the Presidency of Republika Srpska of 30 November, 1992, present: Karadzic, Plavsic, Koljevic, and you, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And turn to item number 3. We find the following -- that's page 2 of the B/C/S. "In response to a parliamentary question, the Presidency discussed whether it was justified to introduce a war commission and an expanded Presidency under the current circumstances. It was established that for well-known reasons a state of war had not been declared and that an expanded Presidency, including the president of the National Assembly and the Prime Minister of Republika Srpska could be introduced only under such circumstances. The same is the -- the case is the same with the War Presidency which was introduced to replace the commission." Actually it has it backwards. It goes on to say: "The law on amendments to the constitutional law of Republika Srpska, which was adopted on June 2nd, 1992, stipulates that during a state of war the Presidency shall be expanded to include the president of the National Assembly and the Prime Minister of Republika Srpska. The same law also stipulates that War Presidencies can be established during a state of war." In both cases, if these institutions are retained, these regulations must be amended and after the words "a state of war," the words, "an imminent threat of war," need to be added. And after the words, "War Presidencies," the words "War Commissions." And then each member of the Presidency spoke about his or her position or work, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'll read it. They probably didn't have the original there, the translation sounded different to me. Can I read the first item and the rest and then you will see that this confirms what I had said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you think there is some sort of translation problem, Mr. Krajisnik, we can have it read again, but the interpreters have the original in B/C/S before them.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they weren't reading from the original, no. May I read the original?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- what portion would you like to read exactly, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 83, number 2, and the rest that the Prosecutor was reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What exactly is your concern about? Where do you have doubts? What --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll read it out. I'll read it out, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which part, Mr. -- Where do you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first sentence worries me, the one here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the first sentence -- okay. You read one sentence that worries you, and that is the first one of item 3, the second item 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'd have to read the whole thing, the whole article, because it was understood differently. "The Presidency discussed whether it was justified to introduce a war commission and an expanded Presidency under the current conditions and in response to a parliamentary question, a question that was put by a Member of Parliament. It was established that a state of war had not been declared for well-known reasons and that it was only under such circumstances that an expanded Presidency, including the president of the National Assembly and the Prime Minister of Republika Srpska could be introduced." I can go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Krajisnik. If -- I invited you if there's any -- if there's a specific concern. We get exactly the same translation as we have on paper at this moment, so therefore there's no need -- if there's any reason to believe that this translation is not correct -- Mr. Josse, I see you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I must be following a different place. That translation certainly wasn't word for word --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sometimes, when it's in response to a parliamentary question, it was put at the end of the sentence rather than at the beginning, but that's structure of sentencing. But where is the major difference between what was just translated and what we find on paper?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I haven't gone so far as to work out what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But of course if I say "Mr. Josse said" or "he said," "he said, Mr. Josse," that of course is the same. You understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. I'm sorry to quibble, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's do the following: Mr. Krajisnik, you have read a major portion and what we received as translation is for 90 -- not substantially different from what we have on paper. If there are any concerns about the translation of this portion, I would allow you to read one line and say here there must be some misunderstanding, but not to read the whole of the document. I don't have it translated in a similar way as before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One other question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is it possible to ask those who are interpreting from English into B/C/S whether, when they were interpreting what Mr. Tieger was reading out in English -- sorry, I've not put that very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do understand. When Mr. Krajisnik read --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger read.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What Mr. Tieger was reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What, then, the question is?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Whether when Mr. Tieger was reading out the English, whether the interpreter was reading from the B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you taking the B/C/S original? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Krajisnik, you couldn't answer that question, I'm afraid -- well, of course, unless you were reading at the same time. When Mr. Tieger's quotations were translated, how was that done?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had the text in B/C/S, but we didn't have the exact paragraph 3, because there are two of them, and it took some time for us to find it, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So therefore you were translating and not following the written translation. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In any event --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One part of it, Your Honour. The first part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So we've covered that now. I think Mr. Krajisnik was looking at the original. I was reading from the written translation of the original. Now we know from the retranslation that that original translation is essentially accurate. I think we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we can move on. Unless there's any need to have the translation of this document be reviewed, of course everyone is -- it's important enough to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the minutes, Mr. Krajisnik, of the Assembly we see a reflection of the existence of the wartime Presidency. In the minutes of the Presidency session we've just read, we see that the question is whether or not that institution explicitly comprised of the Prime Minister and the president of the National Assembly should be retained.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not retained, established. Should it be established. Should it be introduced. That's the only difference. Should you introduce it, not retain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There, of course, I can imagine, therefore I invited you, Mr. Krajisnik, to -- there is a line which starts in English with "In both cases if these institutions are retained ..." that's how it reads. Could you please read that in B/C/S, if you can find it, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'll read it. Of course I'll read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And not any further, just that line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, let me just find this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's at the -- it's on page 7947, seven lines down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "This question remains pending," is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. "In both cases if these institutions are --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. "In both cases, if one stays with these institutions, these regulations should be amended, and after the words 'a state of war --'"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We had as a translation, "If these institutions are retained ..." We now have "If these --" no. "If one stays with these institutions ..." Well, Mr. Krajisnik -- let me ask the interpreters. Is there any possibility that what Mr. Krajisnik tells us, that "If these institutions would be established," that it could be understood in the original as something to be newly established rather than something to be retained or to stay with?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note it is quite ambiguous in the original. It is not "retained" as such. It is not "kept" or "retained," but the original wording, which was now interpreted as "If one stays with," is ambiguous, and that's why the ambiguity was left in English as well. It can be interpreted in different ways. But it is not to introduce for the first time, no. It is not explicitly stated in the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. If you say it's ambiguous, what -- where's the ambiguity exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The wording itself in B/C/S is ambiguous. It is an expression that is ambiguous, "If one stays with ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say you could give that different meanings.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It doesn't say specifically "retained."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That now has been sufficiently clarified, I would say, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I've got a few minutes left, Mr. Krajisnik, so I'm going to ask you a few more questions. Regardless of your position about the existence of the wartime Presidency or the expanded Presidency, the fact is that your position on the Presidency was, in any event, a reflection of your already-existing power at the very apex of the Bosnian Serb leadership structure as we heard from many witnesses, and as we saw reflected in intercepts and documents. So when Dr. Karadzic wanted to discuss who would implement what "we introduced last night," it was you he was talking to. When Mr. Kovacevic, on February 28th at the Deputies Club, when the issue was retaining Bosnian Serb unity and the possibility of Krajina unification with RSK, and he wanted to ensure that that didn't happen, he urged, "our leaders," meaning you and Dr. Karadzic, to go to the Krajina to take care of it. And also, Mr. Krajisnik, when it came to selecting the military figure who would lead the Bosnian Serb forces in the effort to establish Republika Srpska, to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were two people again involved, and that was you and Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, none of that is correct. Actually, it's different, and I can explain all of it, why.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's take it one at a time while we have time. It was you and Dr. Karadzic who were involved in the selection of General Mladic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was present when he talked. I know. You found a quotation. Let me help you so you don't waste any time. We were present in Mr. Kukanjac's office when he talked to Mr. Mladic, and then he thought that he was a good commander. I did not take part in the selection of Mr. Mladic in the least bit. That's what Mr. Karadzic said. I hadn't known of Mr. Mladic before. You can put your next question to me while you find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are you saying that Dr. Karadzic said that you didn't participate in the least bit or that Dr. Karadzic was talking about the selection of Mladic but you were merely -- it may have been misunderstood, because you were merely present.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present in the office, as he said -- Mr. Kukanjac's office when he was looking -- or, rather, when he was listening to what kind of commands Mr. Mladic was issuing. I did not take part in the selection of Mr. Mladic, and no one asked me about it anyway. And at that time, I didn't even know who Mladic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic said at the 50th that you two were there night after night?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you put your questions one at a time, and I'll answer all of them, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just asked you about that: What about Dr. Karadzic's remarks at the 50th that you two were there night after night, selecting him, because -- well, how about that? Let's start there. You spent countless nights Mr. Kukanjac's office. Do you remember that at the 50th?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice. I was with Kukanjac twice in my life. Once he accompanied me home, and the other time was in his office. It wasn't a countless number of times, and I'll give you an answer in terms of how important I was. When Mr. Karadzic left his office, who replaced him? Of course I was only consulted as president of the Assembly, but it was Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Buha who replaced him. I would have replaced him if I were -- I mean, I'm not trying to say that I was the mailman. I was the president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you cited an extract from Mr. Jovic's diary. He also spoke about the selection of General Mladic and the establishment of the VRS, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic said that he informed us that the army of Yugoslavia would leave our area and that I was concerned what the financing would be and how we would manage this, because they had promised us that the JNA would remain in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what he said, and I know that because I read that. Now, was I there as a member of some delegation? Well, perhaps I was. Probably I was. That, yes. But I did not select Mladic. I told you, I was -- well, as Karadzic says, in the gentleman's office when he was commanding somewhere in Kupres, wherever, but I did not take part at all in his selection. I mean, had I taken part in it I would have said so now. I mean, had I been asked then, I could have said I agree, but nobody asked me and I wasn't the one who selected him, and I didn't know that he'd be promoted at all. At that time, however, I did not know anything about Mladic, and I could have said yes, I agree. So -- and if that were the case, I would now say yes, no problem. Mr. Koljevic, Mr. Buha, everybody was in Belgrade when Mr. Jovic was there. It wasn't only me. I don't know who else was there. It doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the question simply was whether Mr. Jovic also spoke about the selection of General Mladic and the establishment of the VRS. That was the question, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the VRS was referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at the time Dr. Karadzic said at the 50th Assembly that General Mladic was selected in part because of his blunt statements in the media, he was also selected because of his efforts in Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic and Mr. Karadzic were in a conflict at the 50th session, and the whole session was in a conflict on account of the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, no. Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know what he stated, but everything he stated is probably written there. I just told you what the reason was. They were in a conflict then. Mr. Karadzic had then replaced Mr. Mladic, so there was this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm asking you isn't it the case that General Mladic was selected, at least in part, because of the fact that he was known for his efforts in Croatia? It's a pretty simple question. You and Dr. Karadzic knew that General Mladic had led forces in Croatia and what he'd done?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we have two different questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first question was whether Mr. Mladic was selected at least in part because that he was known for his efforts in Croatia. Yes or no or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My understanding was because he had asserted himself as a soldier. Probably because he was in war in Croatia. He was well known in the media as a good soldier. That was probably the case. That's what Karadzic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Dr. Karadzic knew full well what was happening in Croatia, as reflected in the intercept with Gojko Djogo on October 12, 1991, that we've heard, where Dr. Karadzic said -- talked about the carnage in Croatia, saying that 40.000 had died and less than a thousand Serb.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know. I would have to try to remember. Karadzic would not have selected him for that. Because he was a war criminal? Because of that? I'm not going to comment on a later period, but he selected him as a good soldier, a good military leader, whatever, and somebody probably from the Yugoslav People's Army put his name forth as a proposal. He became commander of the 2nd Military District and then he took over as commander of the Main Staff in Sarajevo. He replaced over Kukanjac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He was selected to lead the effort on behalf -- the military effort on behalf of Republika Srpska, to divide what you once called, in the Club 91 interview, the live tissue of Bosnia. And that would be done, Mr. Krajisnik -- that necessitated the establishment of divided areas that would be Muslim, Serb, and Croat; that is areas that would be pure Serb areas, as you said on February 28th at the Deputies' Club, or areas that would be clean, as you said at the 34th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained what I meant when I said clean areas. Ethnic, ethnic Serb areas, that we shouldn't take the areas that belonged to others. I explained that question. I'll tell you about Mladic. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With respect, you have explained the pure territories. Let me just play a quick clip of you speaking about the clean territories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you play that, and of course I take it there's a question related to that, and then we should finish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear anything. I really don't know what's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we restart so that the B/C/S is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just hope that Mr. Krajisnik will have an opportunity to deal with this properly. In other words, a question will follow and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. No, I suggested that just playing the video is not what I --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The sound seems to be problematic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt, but there's clearly French translation but no English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The English booth cannot hear the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's dispense with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing I wanted to do is to just wait and see whether Mr. Krajisnik can hear anything at all. But we have now talked all through this video clip seven times, so everybody will have lost track.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll move forward. We have the transcript, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have the transcript. Of course there should be a possibility to check whether this transcript reflects what has been said. Mr. Krajisnik, do you remember the occasion when this was filmed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read this transcript, so I can answer, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear any of this, but never mind. I am going to answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There must have been a moment when someone could hear it otherwise it wouldn't have been transcribed and translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is taken from that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not going to dispute that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then please put your questions to Mr. Krajisnik, who says that he has read the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I put to you before the -- your remark -- well, here you say, put it this way, after the suggestion by Mr. Kasagic that Sarajevo should be traded for the Banja Luka area, and you intervene and object, and you chastise him, and then you say, about 12 lines down from the beginning of your comments: "If you want me to say so, gentlemen, the Muslims, the Croats sought, and the Muslims a municipality in Banja Luka, and we did not accept it because that territory of ours must be clean." On February 28th, you told the deputies that everything you do is for pure territories. Those comments, Mr. Krajisnik, reflected what was necessary to divide what you had once called the live tissue of Bosnia, an effort that would --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is clearly stated here that the Muslims wanted a municipality in Banja Luka. The Muslims and the Croats are there. I said that we were against those municipalities, want to have our territory without Muslim municipalities. This has to do with the Vance-Owen Plan, because they want to give Sarajevo for some municipalities in Krajina. And when I say "clean territories," I mean they should be annexed to Republika Srpska, not that the Muslims and Croats should be cleansed. I mean, we want to have clean territories, no Muslim municipalities there when there's few of them and, on the other hand, 150.000 Serbs. It has nothing to do with ethnic cleansing. And I did not think about ethnic cleansing then, and it doesn't say so here. 150.000 Serbs for 15 municipalities, they want Glamoc, Grahovo, because there was this discussion of the Vance-Owen Plan. You see that. It's 1993. It has nothing to do with ethnic cleansing, no ethnic cleansing and no clean territories where somebody would have to be expelled. I know this exactly. When the people from Krajina said we're going to give Sarajevo so we'd get some municipalities in Krajina, and I said no, we advocated both when I talked about the negotiations. This is about negotiations, not about ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, this was your last question, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this concludes the cross-examination. After the weekend, on Monday -- and Mr. Registrar, we are sitting next week --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: In the afternoon in the same courtroom, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, there will be re-examination by Mr. Josse, there may be further questions by the Bench -- you are familiar with the procedure. Mr. Josse, perhaps if that would assist you, there's always a small chance that if one expects the priority list to be translated by next Monday morning, you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We've got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've got it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was instructed not to express myself over-optimistic but that there was a small chance that it would be ready by today, so therefore I raised the matter, but it's good to hear that it's there already. Yes, Mr. Krajisnik, although we have to be brief because there is a videolink this afternoon in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One second. Can I bring on Monday a decision on abolishing the Presidency in the Assembly? That's the 12th of December, 1992. Can I bring it in Monday, and can I submit it to you so that you see what it was that we abolished at the Assembly; was it a War Presidency or a commission, so that you could see what existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, at least what was abolished. That doesn't mean that you abolish everything that exists, but -- Mr. Josse --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course you always can bring it, and then of course we have to see how to deal with the translation issues at that very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I'd encourage that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please bring it, Mr. Krajisnik. Decisions have the advantage that they are usually a bit shorter than minutes. If nothing else, if we don't need to discuss anything else before this weekend, I wish everyone a good weekend, and we'll adjourn until quarter past two, same courtroom next Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
